english: Dad goes to the mountains every Sunday.
tip: -세요 respects the subject: 아빠는 가세요 (gaseyo); for yourself, 가요.

english: I don't like high mountains.
tip: 높아요 (nopayo) can end a sentence, but in front of a noun the adjective flips to -(으)ㄴ (-(eu)n): 높은 산 (nopeun san) = a high mountain.

english: I go to the gym every morning.
tip: 헬스장 (helseujang) = gym — Konglish, from English 'health'.

english: I do yoga twice a week.
tip: 번 (beon) counts times, with native numbers: 두 번 (du beon) = twice.

english: I was too tired today, so I rested.
tip: -아/어서 = so, because: 피곤해서 쉬었어요 (pigonhaeseo) = tired, so I rested.

english: I went to watch a baseball game.
tip: -(으)러 가다 = go to (do): 보러 갔어요 (boreo gasseoyo) = went to watch.

english: I like baseball more than soccer.
tip: 보다 (boda = than) attaches to the thing you like less, and it comes first: 축구보다 야구를 (chukguboda yagureul) = baseball more than soccer – reverse of English order.

english: Do you play tennis often?
tip: 치다 (chida) = hit — for tennis, badminton, piano, guitar: 테니스를 쳐요.

english: I saw three movies last month.
tip: 편 (pyeon) counts films: 세 편 (se pyeon) = three (movies).

english: I like comedies.
tip: 좋아해요 (joahaeyo = like) takes 을/를 (eul/reul): 영화를 좋아해요 (yeonghwareul joahaeyo). 좋아요 (joayo = is good) would need 이/가 (i/ga) instead.

english: I can't watch a movie without popcorn.
tip: 없이 (eopsi) = without: 팝콘 없이 = without popcorn.

target: 드라마 한 시즌을 하루 만에 다 봤어요.
english: I binged a whole season in one day.
tip: 만에 (mane) = in (just): 하루 만에 = in a single day.

english: I'm reading an interesting book these days.
tip: 있다·없다 adjectives take -는: 재미있는 책 (jaemiinneun chaek) = an interesting book; other adjectives take -(으)ㄴ (예쁜).

target: 한 달에 책을 두 권 읽어요.
english: I read two books a month.
tip: 권 (gwon) counts books: 두 권 (du gwon) = two books.

english: I read a little before bed.
tip: V-기 전에 = before V-ing: 자기 전에 (jagi jeone) = before sleeping.

target: 어제 밤에 게임을 세 시간 했어요.
english: I played games for three hours last night.
tip: 시간 (sigan) counts hours, native numbers: 세 시간 = three hours.

english: My friend is really good at games.
tip: 'Good at games' takes a direct object in Korean: 게임을 잘해요 (geimeul jalhaeyo) – 잘하다 (jalhada) treats the skill as something you do to the game, no 'at'.

english: This time I won.
tip: 제가 (jega) = 저 + subject marker 가: 제가 이겼어요 = I won.

english: Our son does nothing but game.
tip: 만 (man) = only: 게임만 해요 = only plays games.

english: We sang for two hours at karaoke.
tip: 동안 (dongan) = for, during: 두 시간 동안 = for two hours.

english: I can't sing well.
tip: 잘 못 (jal mot) = can't do well: 잘 못 불러요 = can't sing well.

english: I blow off stress at karaoke.
tip: 스트레스를 풀다 (pulda) = relieve stress, lit. 'untie' it: 스트레스를 풀어요.

english: Taking photos is my hobby.
tip: A -기 (-gi) phrase is a full noun and takes particles like one: 사진 찍기가 (sajin jjikgiga) puts the subject marker 가 (ga) right on 'photo-taking'.

english: I took a hundred photos on the trip.
tip: Flat things get the counter 장 (jang) – photos, tickets, paper: 사진을 백 장 (sajineul baek jang) = a hundred photos, literally 'photos, hundred flat-things'.

english: I shoot with my phone more than my camera.
tip: 보다 (boda) alone means 'than' – 더 (deo = more) just adds stress: 카메라보다 더 자주 (kameraboda deo jaju) = more often than the camera.

english: I take a photography class.
tip: -(으)러 (-(eu)reo) + a motion verb = go somewhere to do it: 배우러 다녀요 (baeureo danyeoyo) = attend in order to learn. Only works with going-verbs like 가다 (gada).

english: Did you have a good weekend?
tip: 주말 잘 보냈어요? (jumal jal bonaesseoyo?) — the standard Monday greeting.

english: I did absolutely nothing this weekend.
tip: 아무것도 + 안 = nothing: 아무것도 안 했어요 (amugeotdo an haesseoyo).

english: If the weather's nice, I'll go hiking.
tip: 'If' is an ending, not a word: -(으)면 (-(eu)myeon) glues onto the verb – 날씨가 좋으면 (nalssiga joeumyeon) = if the weather is good. No separate 'if' anywhere.

english: What's your KakaoTalk ID?
tip: 카톡 (katok) = KakaoTalk, Korea's default messenger – and it works as a verb: 카톡해요 (katokhaeyo) = text me. Brand names verbify freely with 하다 (hada).
